# What Rationality Alone Gives You

## Where We Left Off

Nash equilibrium says each player is playing a best response to what the others are actually doing.

. . .

That is two claims bundled together. Each player is **rational**, and each player's beliefs about the others are **correct**.

. . .

Rationality we can defend. Where does the second one come from?

## Two Assumptions

Nobody hands the players a copy of the equilibrium before the game starts.

. . .

In the games we have solved, we found the equilibrium by doing the algebra ourselves, and then assumed the players had found it too.

. . .

Today's question: if all we assume is that everyone is rational, and everyone knows everyone is rational, and so on up, what can we conclude?

## The Answer, In Advance

Much less than Nash equilibrium.

. . .

What common knowledge of rationality delivers is a weaker notion, **rationalizability**.

. . .

Every Nash equilibrium strategy is rationalizable. Plenty of rationalizable strategies are in no Nash equilibrium at all.

# Rationalizability

## Best Responses, Again

A strategy is a **best response** to a belief about what the other player will do if nothing else does better against that belief.

. . .

We met a version of this in the notes at 3.3, under the name 'iterated best response'. Now we state it properly.

## The Definition

Here is the definition, in two parts.

::: {.callout-tip title="Rationalizability"}
A **class** of strategies is rationalizable if every member of the class is a best response, assuming the probability that every other player plays some strategy from the class is 1.

A **strategy** is rationalizable if it belongs to some rationalizable class.
:::

. . .

Note what is doing the work. The class has to support itself.

## Why the Circularity is the Point

It looks circular, and it is, but that is a feature.

. . .

The idea is that you can defend playing $s$ by saying "I played $s$ because I expected them to play $t$".

. . .

And then you can be asked to defend expecting $t$. And you can answer: because they would have expected me to play $s'$. And so on.

. . .

A class is rationalizable when the chain of defences never has to leave the class. Nobody is ever asked to justify a belief they cannot justify.

## What This Rules Out

Not much, in some games. But not nothing.

. . .

A strictly dominated strategy is never a best response to anything, so it is never rationalizable.

. . .

In fact, in a two-player game, the rationalizable strategies are exactly the ones that survive iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies.

. . .

With one wrinkle: a strategy counts as dominated if some **mixture** beats it, not just if another pure strategy does. Last week's machinery earns its keep here.

. . .

So Lecture 3's technique and today's concept are the same thing seen from two sides.

# Where the Two Come Apart

## Every Nash Strategy is Rationalizable

Take any Nash equilibrium. Consider the class consisting of just the strategies in it.

. . .

Each is a best response to the others, by the definition of equilibrium. So the class is rationalizable, so each member is rationalizable.

. . .

That direction is easy. The interesting direction is the other one.

## A Game With No Pure Equilibrium

|         | a         | b         |
|--------:|:---------:|:---------:|
| **A**   | **5**, 0  | 0, **1**  |
| **B**   | 0, **1**  | **1**, 0  |

: A game with no pure strategy equilibria {#tbl-rat-no-pure}

. . .

No cell has both payoffs bolded, so there is no pure strategy equilibrium. Familiar territory.

## The Equilibrium

There is exactly one Nash equilibrium.

. . .

Row plays $\langle A, \frac{1}{2}; B, \frac{1}{2} \rangle$. Column plays $\langle a, \frac{1}{6}; b, \frac{5}{6} \rangle$.

. . .

Row's expected payoff is $\frac{5}{6}$; Column's is $\frac{1}{2}$.

. . .

So Principle 1, that rational players play their part of a Nash equilibrium, says there is exactly one rational thing for each player to do.

## But Everything is Rationalizable

Look at the bolding again. $A$ is a best response to $a$. And $a$ is a best response to $B$. And $B$ is a best response to $b$. And $b$ is a best response to $A$.

. . .

That is a closed cycle. So $\{A, B\}$ and $\{a, b\}$ form a rationalizable class.

. . .

Every strategy in this game is rationalizable, including every mixture. For any strategy you like, there is some opposing strategy it is a best response to.

## Two Principles

1. Rational players always play some part of a Nash equilibrium strategy.
2. Rational players always play rationalizable strategies.

. . .

On @tbl-rat-no-pure, Principle 1 rules out all but one strategy per player. Principle 2 says anything goes.

. . .

Which is right?

# Is Nash Self-Undermining?

## The Repeated Case is Easy

If the game is played many times, Principle 1 looks right.

. . .

Playing $A$ every time will be a disaster for Row. After a while Column picks up what is going on and responds with $b$.

. . .

In a repeated game, randomising is the right thing to do. But that is a fact about repeated games.

## The One-Shot Case

Here is an argument that Principle 1 undermines itself.

. . .

Assume the only rational thing to do is play the equilibrium strategy. So Row flips a coin.

. . .

Column knows what rationality is, so Column knows Row will flip a coin.

. . .

But now Column is not playing a game. Column is facing a decision problem against a known chance device.

## The Sting

Against Row's coin flip, every one of Column's options has the same expected return.

. . .

So every option is equally rational. So Column can rationally do anything.

. . .

Which is exactly what Principle 2 says, and exactly what Principle 1 denied.

## Stated Generally

In any game whose only equilibrium is a mixed one, these three cannot all be true.

. . .

**A.** Only strategies that are part of Nash equilibria are rational, and all players know this.

**B.** All players are rational, and all players know this.

**C.** Any strategy known to have the same expected return as a rational strategy can be rationally played.

## The Derivation

By (A) and (B), the other player will play a mixed strategy.

. . .

But then every strategy in the support of your own mixture has equal expected return. We proved that last week; it is how we found the mixture.

. . .

So by (C) the pure strategies are as rational as the mixture. Which contradicts (A).

## Which One Goes?

Conventional wisdom in the game theory texts is that **(C)** fails.

. . .

Principle 2 says that **(A)** fails.

. . .

I am not going to take a stand. What I want you to see is that there is a genuine clash between the idea that Nash equilibria have a special role in rational choice, and the principle that rational agents maximise expected utility.

# Three-Way Games

## Why Two Options Hide the Difference

With two choices each, the argument between the Principles comes down to a narrow question. Is randomising **obligatory**, or is playing a pure strategy from the support **permissible**?

. . .

That is hard to have intuitions about, because it is tangled up with the metaphysics of mixed strategies from last week.

. . .

With three choices, the two come apart much further.

## A Three-Way Game

|         | a         | b         | c            |
|--------:|:---------:|:---------:|:------------:|
| **A**   | **3**, 0  | 0, **3**  | 0, 2         |
| **B**   | 0, **3**  | **3**, 0  | 0, 2         |
| **C**   | 2, 0      | 2, 0      | **1**, **1** |

: A three-way game with a poor pure strategy equilibrium {#tbl-rat-payout-1}

. . .

One cell has both payoffs bolded. $Cc$ is the unique Nash equilibrium, and it pays 1 to each.

## The Cycle Again

$A$ is a best response to $a$. $a$ is a best response to $B$. $B$ is a best response to $b$. $b$ is a best response to $A$.

. . .

So $A$, $B$, $a$ and $b$ are all rationalizable, even though none of them appears in any equilibrium.

## And No Mixed Equilibrium Either

You might expect a mixed equilibrium over those four strategies. There isn't one.

. . .

The only candidate is each player splitting 50/50 between their first two options.

. . .

But against that, reciprocating returns $1.5$, while the third option returns $2$. So both players defect to the third option, and the candidate collapses.

. . .

One equilibrium, pure or mixed. All nine strategies rationalizable.

## Now Raise the Stakes

The same game, with the equilibrium payoff raised from 1 to 2.

|         | a         | b         | c            |
|--------:|:---------:|:---------:|:------------:|
| **A**   | **3**, 0  | 0, **3**  | 0, 2         |
| **B**   | 0, **3**  | **3**, 0  | 0, 2         |
| **C**   | 2, 0      | 2, 0      | **2**, **2** |

: The same game with the equilibrium raised to 2 {#tbl-rat-payout-2}

. . .

Again $Cc$ is the unique equilibrium. Again everything is rationalizable.

## Does Your Intuition Move?

In both games, playing $A$ or $B$ is rationalizable and is not part of any equilibrium.

. . .

For what it is worth, my intuition says that playing $A$ or $B$ is rational when the alternative is an equilibrium paying 1, and not when the alternative is a guaranteed 2.

. . .

But that is an intuition about payoffs, not about rationality, and the two games are identical in every structural respect.

## Where That Leaves Us

We wanted the cases to settle which Principle is right. They do not.

. . .

What they do is make the stakes vivid. Could it ever be rational, under common knowledge of rationality, to play $A$ or $B$ in either of these games?

. . .

If yes, Nash equilibrium is not what rationality requires. If no, we need to say what rules it out, given that every step of the defence checks out.

## Next Time

Everything so far has been simultaneous. Both players move at once, or may as well have.

. . .

Next week we let players move in sequence, and see what changes when one player can watch the other first.
